lessons.title: Structure of a C Program
lessons.overview: A C program consists of preprocessor directives, global declarations, and functions. Every C program must have a main() function — that's where execution begins. Understanding the structure is the first step to writing C programs.
keyConcepts: Preprocessor directives: #include <stdio.h> includes the standard I/O library
main() function: the entry point of every C program — execution starts here
Statements: each statement ends with a semicolon (;)
Curly braces { } define blocks of code
return 0; indicates successful program termination
printf() prints output to the screen; scanf() reads input from the keyboard
Comments: // single line, /* multi line */ — ignored by the compiler
formulas: Program structure: #include → global vars → functions → main()
printf format: printf("format string", variables);
scanf format: scanf("format string", &variables);  (note the & for address)

tables.title: Common printf/scanf Format Specifiers
tables.note: Forgetting the & in scanf is a common error: scanf("%d", &num), NOT scanf("%d", num).

codeExamples.title: Your First C Program — Hello World with Input
codeExamples.explanation: This program asks for the user's name and age, then prints a greeting. Note: scanf needs & for int but not for string (array name is already a pointer). The \n creates a new line.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the & in scanf for non-array variables: scanf("%d", &num) not scanf("%d", num)
Missing semicolons at the end of statements
Using %d for float or %f for int — format specifier must match the data type
Forgetting #include <stdio.h> when using printf/scanf
examTips: Every C program MUST have a main() function
Remember the & in scanf for int, float, char — but NOT for string arrays
Format specifiers: %d=int, %f=float, %c=char, %s=string
Always return 0 at the end of main() to indicate success

practiceQuestions.question: Which function is the entry point of a C program?
practiceQuestions.explanation: main() is the entry point. Execution begins at the first statement inside main(). Every C program must have exactly one main() function.

practiceQuestions.question: What is wrong with: scanf("%d", num); where num is an int?
practiceQuestions.explanation: scanf needs the ADDRESS of the variable, not its value. For int variables, you must use &num: scanf("%d", &num). The & is the 'address-of' operator. Arrays (strings) are exceptions because the array name is already an address.

practiceQuestions.question: Which format specifier is used to print a float value?
practiceQuestions.explanation: %f is used for float and double. %d is for int, %c is for char, %s is for string (char array).

lessons.title: Data Types, Variables, and Operators
lessons.overview: C has several built-in data types for storing different kinds of data: int for integers, float for decimals, char for characters, and more. Operators perform operations on variables and values — arithmetic, relational, logical, and assignment operators.
keyConcepts: int: whole numbers (4 bytes, range -2³¹ to 2³¹-1). Modifiers: short, long, unsigned.
float: single-precision decimal (4 bytes, ~7 digits). double: double-precision (8 bytes, ~15 digits).
char: single character (1 byte). Stored as ASCII integer internally.
Arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, % (modulo — remainder of division)
Relational operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= (return 1 for true, 0 for false)
Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)
Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=
Increment/decrement: ++ (add 1), -- (subtract 1). Pre: ++x (increment then use). Post: x++ (use then increment).
formulas: Size: int=4 bytes, float=4 bytes, double=8 bytes, char=1 byte
Integer division: 7/2 = 3 (not 3.5!) — both operands are int, so result is int
Modulo: 7 % 2 = 1 (remainder of 7÷2)
Type casting: (float)7/2 = 3.5 — cast one operand to float before division

tables.title: C Data Types
tables.note: Sizes may vary by platform. Use sizeof(type) to check on your system.

tables.title: Operator Precedence (high to low)
tables.note: Higher precedence operators are evaluated first. Use parentheses to override.

diagrams.title: Pre vs Post Increment
diagrams.content:
Pre-increment (++x): increment FIRST, then use
  int x = 5;
  int y = ++x;  // x becomes 6, y = 6

Post-increment (x++): use FIRST, then increment
  int x = 5;
  int y = x++;  // y = 5, then x becomes 6

  x: 5 → 6    x: 5 → 6
  y: 6         y: 5

codeExamples.title: Operators in Action
codeExamples.explanation: Note that 10/3 = 3 (integer division — the decimal part is truncated). To get a decimal result, cast one operand to float: (float)10/3 = 3.33. Also note the difference between x++ (post) and ++x (pre).

commonMistakes: Using / for integer division expecting a decimal result: 7/2 = 3, not 3.5
Confusing = (assignment) with == (comparison): if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x, it doesn't compare!
Using % with float/double — modulo only works with integers
Forgetting that relational operators return 1 (true) or 0 (false), not 'true'/'false'
examTips: Integer division: 7/2 = 3 (not 3.5). Cast to float: (float)7/2 = 3.5
= is assignment, == is comparison. This is a very common exam question!
Pre-increment (++x): change then use. Post-increment (x++): use then change.
Know the operator precedence: * / % before + -, relational before &&, && before ||
sizeof(int) = 4 bytes, sizeof(char) = 1 byte, sizeof(float) = 4 bytes

practiceQuestions.question: What is the output of: int a = 7, b = 2; printf("%d", a / b);
practiceQuestions.explanation: Since both a and b are int, integer division is performed. 7/2 = 3 (the decimal part is truncated, not rounded). To get 3.5, you'd need: (float)7/2.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the difference between x++ and ++x?
options: x++ increments after use, ++x increments before use
x++ is for float, ++x is for int
practiceQuestions.explanation: x++ (post-increment): use the current value first, then increment. ++x (pre-increment): increment first, then use the new value. Example: int x=5; int y=x++ gives y=5, x=6. int y=++x gives y=6, x=6.

practiceQuestions.question: What does the expression (5 > 3) && (2 < 1) evaluate to?
practiceQuestions.explanation: (5 > 3) is true (1). (2 < 1) is false (0). 1 && 0 = 0 (false). The AND operator requires BOTH conditions to be true.

lessons.title: Decision Making — if-else and switch
lessons.overview: Control structures allow a program to make decisions and repeat actions. The if-else statement executes different code based on a condition. The switch statement selects one of many code blocks based on a value. These are the building blocks of logic in C.
keyConcepts: if: execute code only if a condition is true
if-else: execute one block if true, another if false
if-else if-else: check multiple conditions in order
switch: select one of many blocks based on a single value (int or char only)
break in switch: exits the switch — without it, execution falls through to the next case
default in switch: executed if no case matches
Ternary operator: condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false (shorthand for if-else)
formulas: if: if (condition) { /* code */ }
if-else: if (condition) { /* A */ } else { /* B */ }
switch: switch (var) { case 1: ...; break; case 2: ...; break; default: ...; }
Ternary: result = (a > b) ? a : b;

tables.title: if-else vs switch
rows: int and char only (not float or string)
No (each case is a single value)
tables.note: Use switch for menu-driven programs. Use if-else for complex conditions and ranges.

codeExamples.title: Grade Calculator using if-else if
codeExamples.explanation: The conditions are checked top to bottom. The first true condition's block is executed, and the rest are skipped. The final 'else' is the fallback when no condition matches.

codeExamples.title: Simple Calculator using switch
codeExamples.explanation: switch checks the operator character. Each case handles one operator. break prevents fall-through. default handles invalid operators. Note the division-by-zero check inside the '/' case.

commonMistakes: Using = instead of == in conditions: if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x (always true!)
Forgetting break in switch — causes fall-through to the next case
Not using curly braces for multi-statement if blocks
Using switch with float or string — switch only works with int and char
examTips: ALWAYS use == for comparison, not =. if (x == 5) compares, if (x = 5) assigns.
Don't forget break in switch cases! Without it, execution falls through.
switch can only test equality with int and char — not float, not ranges
The ternary operator is a shorthand: grade = (marks >= 40) ? 'P' : 'F';

practiceQuestions.question: What happens if you forget 'break' in a switch case?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without break, execution falls through to the next case's code, even if that case doesn't match. This is called 'fall-through'. Sometimes it's intentional, but usually it's a bug.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the value of x after: int x = 5; if (x = 10) { x++; }
practiceQuestions.explanation: x = 10 is an ASSIGNMENT, not a comparison! It assigns 10 to x and evaluates to 10 (non-zero = true). So the if block executes: x becomes 11. This is a classic bug — use == for comparison.

practiceQuestions.question: Which data type can NOT be used in a switch statement?
practiceQuestions.explanation: switch only works with integer types (int, char, short, long). float and double cannot be used because switch tests exact equality, which is unreliable with floating-point numbers.

lessons.title: Loops — for, while, and do-while
lessons.overview: Loops repeat a block of code multiple times. The 'for' loop is used when you know the number of iterations. The 'while' loop checks the condition BEFORE executing (may run 0 times). The 'do-while' loop checks AFTER executing (runs at least once). Loops are essential for processing arrays, generating patterns, and repeating calculations.
keyConcepts: for loop: for (init; condition; update) { } — used when count is known
while loop: while (condition) { } — checks BEFORE, may not execute at all
do-while loop: do { } while (condition) — checks AFTER, runs at least once
break: exits the loop immediately
continue: skips the rest of the current iteration, goes to the next
Nested loops: a loop inside another loop — used for 2D patterns, matrix operations
Infinite loop: condition is always true — use break to exit
formulas: for: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { /* runs n times */ }
while: while (condition) { /* runs while true */ }
do-while: do { /* runs at least once */ } while (condition);
Nested loop iterations: outer × inner = total iterations

tables.title: Comparison of Loop Types
rows: Unknown count, run at least once
tables.note: All three loops can be converted to each other, but each has its most natural use case.

diagrams.title: Loop Flow Comparison
diagrams.content:
for/while (check first):          do-while (check last):

  ┌─────────┐                     ┌─────────┐
  │ condition│──false──→ exit      │  body    │
  └────┬────┘                     └────┬────┘
       │ true                          │
  ┌────▼────┐                     ┌────▼────┐
  │  body    │                     │ condition│──false──→ exit
  └────┬────┘                     └────┬────┘
       │                               │ true
  └─────── back to condition    ┌─────── back to body

Key: do-while ALWAYS runs the body at least once.

codeExamples.title: Three Loops — Same Task (Print 1 to 5)
codeExamples.explanation: All three produce the same output. The for loop is the most compact. The while loop separates initialization, condition, and update. The do-while guarantees at least one execution even if the condition is false initially.

codeExamples.title: Star Pattern using Nested Loops
codeExamples.explanation: The outer loop controls rows (1 to 5). The inner loop controls columns (1 to i). In row 1, print 1 star. In row 2, print 2 stars. And so on. The inner loop's limit depends on the outer loop variable — this is the key to triangular patterns.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to update the loop variable in while/do-while — causes infinite loop
Off-by-one error: for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) runs n+1 times, not n. Use i < n.
Forgetting the semicolon after while in do-while: do { } while (cond); ← the ; is required
Infinite loop: while (1) { } or for (;;) { } — use break to exit
examTips: for loop: use when you know the exact number of iterations
while: check before, may run 0 times. do-while: check after, runs at least once.
Don't forget the semicolon after while in do-while: } while (cond);
break exits the loop. continue skips to the next iteration.
For nested loops, total iterations = outer_count × inner_count

practiceQuestions.question:
How many times does this loop run?
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { }
practiceQuestions.explanation: i goes from 0, 1, 2, ..., 9. That's 10 values (0 through 9). The condition i < 10 is true for i=0..9, false when i=10. So the loop body executes 10 times.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the minimum number of times a do-while loop executes?
practiceQuestions.explanation: do-while checks the condition AFTER executing the body. So even if the condition is false initially, the body runs at least once. This is the key difference from while (which can run 0 times).

practiceQuestions.question: What does 'continue' do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and goes to the next
Restarts the loop from the beginning
practiceQuestions.explanation: continue skips the remaining code in the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration. break exits the loop entirely. For example: for(i=0;i<5;i++){if(i==2)continue;printf("%d",i);} prints 0134 (skips 2).

lessons.title: Functions — Definition, Declaration, and Call
lessons.overview: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Functions help organize code, avoid repetition, and make programs modular. C programs are collections of functions that call each other. The main() function is where execution starts.
keyConcepts: Function declaration (prototype): tells the compiler about the function's name, return type, and parameters
Function definition: the actual implementation — contains the code that runs
Function call: invokes the function, passing arguments
Return type: the type of value the function returns (int, float, void, etc.)
Parameters (formal): variables in the function definition that receive values
Arguments (actual): values passed to the function when calling it
Call by value: a COPY of the argument is passed — changes inside the function don't affect the original
Call by reference: the ADDRESS of the argument is passed — changes inside the function DO affect the original
Recursion: a function that calls itself — needs a base case to stop
formulas: Declaration: returnType functionName(paramType param);
Definition: returnType functionName(paramType param) { /* code */ return value; }
Call: functionName(arguments);
Call by value: void func(int x) — x is a copy
Call by reference: void func(int *x) — x is the address

tables.title: Call by Value vs Call by Reference
rows: When you don't want to modify the original
When you want to modify the original or pass large data
tables.note: Arrays are ALWAYS passed by reference in C (the array name decays to a pointer).

codeExamples.title: Call by Value vs Call by Reference
codeExamples.explanation: swapByValue receives copies of x and y — swapping the copies doesn't affect the originals. swapByReference receives the addresses (&x, &y) and swaps the values at those addresses — the originals ARE changed.

codeExamples.title: Recursion — Factorial
codeExamples.explanation: Recursion has two parts: (1) the base case (n <= 1 → return 1) that stops the recursion, and (2) the recursive case (n * factorial(n-1)) that reduces the problem. Without a base case, recursion never stops — stack overflow!

commonMistakes: Forgetting the function prototype (declaration) before main() if the function is defined after main()
Forgetting the & when calling by reference: func(&x), not func(x)
Missing base case in recursion — causes infinite recursion and stack overflow
Not returning a value from a non-void function — undefined behavior
examTips: Call by value: changes DON'T affect the original. Call by reference: changes DO.
Arrays are always passed by reference in C (array name = pointer to first element)
Recursion needs a base case — without it, infinite recursion → stack overflow
Function prototype tells the compiler about the function before it's used
Know how to trace recursion: draw the call stack and work backwards

practiceQuestions.question: In call by value, what happens to the original variable?
options: It is copied to a new variable
practiceQuestions.explanation: Call by value passes a COPY of the argument. Any changes made inside the function affect only the copy, not the original variable. The original remains unchanged.

practiceQuestions.question: What is required to prevent infinite recursion?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A base case is a condition that stops the recursion (e.g., if (n <= 1) return 1;). Without it, the function calls itself forever, eventually causing a stack overflow.

practiceQuestions.question: How are arrays passed to functions in C?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Arrays are always passed by reference in C. When you pass an array name, it decays to a pointer to the first element. Changes made inside the function affect the original array.
